taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO as Prunus mexicana S.Watson. Older varietal and segregate names are synonyms under the accepted species concept.
look_here_first: Start with the bark and spur shoots. Mexican plum is a small deciduous tree with gray to orange-brown bark, alternate simple serrate leaves, and clusters of fragrant white flowers on short lateral spur shoots. Then confirm the Rosaceae hypanthium, many free stamens, single superior ovary, and a glaucous purple-gray drupe.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Travis — UT Plant Resources Center Rosaceae index documents three Travis County Prunus mexicana specimens. Williamson — UT PRC Vascular Plants of Williamson County provides a detailed local treatment. Comal — Harvard University Herbaria specimen GH 01722647 was collected at Anhalt, Texas; the Handbook of Texas places Anhalt in western Comal County.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: The Purola Preserve Hays County plant is documented as introduced from a native plant nursery and is deliberately excluded from native-county evidence.

best_field_traits: bark gray with horizontal lenticels on typical stems, becoming orange-brown and fissured on larger trunks
leaves alternate, simple, serrate, stipulate, often short-hairy/velvety when young
flowers in small umbel-like clusters on short lateral spur shoots
5 white petals arising from the rim of a bell-shaped hypanthium
about 30 free stamens in several series
single superior one-chambered ovary with one ovule
fruit a round glaucous purple-gray drupe with a single stone
morphology_keys.leaves: Alternate simple leaves with early-deciduous stipules; blades broadly elliptic to ovate/obovate and serrate.
morphology_keys.flower: Five petals and many stamens arise from a conspicuous hypanthium; the single pistil sits free inside rather than being fused to the hypanthium.
morphology_keys.fruit: One superior ovary becomes one drupe with a single hard endocarp/stone.
morphology_keys.family_training: Excellent Rosaceae comparison against Rubus trivialis: both show a hypanthium and many stamens, but Prunus has one carpel becoming one drupe while Rubus has many free carpels becoming an aggregate of drupelets.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Use tree habit, pubescent broad leaves, spur-shoot flower clusters, hypanthium and mature single-stone drupe together. Do not use white spring flowers alone.
